Keeping people safe

Security in an open city.

A stadium has a clear boundary. A city-wide event has to protect the ceremony while the surrounding city keeps moving.

Protection has to work with movement.

These parts are connected. A strong boundary matters, but people must still be able to move and reach help.

Manage access across spaces

A ceremony across riverbanks and streets has many points where event activity meets the public city. Access needs to be managed across those spaces.

The central security challenge is to protect the event without blocking safe movement or help.

The whole picture

One route connects many systems.

The river, audience movement, safety response and live show all depend on one another. A change in one part can ripple through the rest.

Where pressure can build

The big risks live between the parts.

Each challenge is manageable on its own. The hard part is how one change can affect another team, another route or the timing of the show.

01 / PLACE≈

Water and weather change the plan.

Rain and river conditions can affect safe navigation, rehearsals, surfaces and equipment. That can leave less room to test a change before the live moment.

02 / MOVEMENT↗

People need to keep moving safely.

Arrivals, access checks, crossings and accessible routes all have to fit together. A slow point can send queues elsewhere or make it harder to reach someone who needs help.

03 / COORDINATION⌁

Many teams share one picture.

Different teams look after connected parts of the city and the show. If information or decisions arrive out of step, people may respond to different versions of the situation.

04 / LIVE SHOW✳

There is little time to fix a late surprise.

A live ceremony has a fixed moment. A technical problem, delay or change in conditions can affect the audience experience and the broadcast before there is time to reset.

What resilience looks like

Plan for change, not perfection.

Good planning cannot remove every uncertainty. It can make problems easier to notice, easier to share and safer to respond to.

01

Test the hand-offs.

Practice how routes, teams, equipment and timing work together—not just each piece on its own.

02

Share one clear picture.

Make sure the people making decisions and guiding the public can act on the same current information.

03

Keep a way to adapt.

Agree what can change, who can decide, and how to protect people if the original plan no longer fits.

The most important plan is the one that connects the plans.

A city-wide ceremony succeeds through many small decisions that meet at the right moment. The clearest way to understand its risks is to follow those connections.
